$description: The Inspector dock's own chrome, as a Jx document over the kit: a header naming the tab and what the dock is pointed at, a real `tablist` of three tabs (Page · Element · Assistant, specs/studio.md §6), and a `tabpanel` per tab. It draws no tab BODY: each of the five leaves (the Page tab's body, Element's Content, Style and Logic, and the Assistant) is a mounted document of its own, so each leaf carries one empty `[part="panel-body"]` island the adapter announces through `onNodeCreated` (studio-ui-guidelines.md §9.4). Element hosts three leaves behind a sub-switch, a single-select `jx-action-group` inside its panel; the other two tabs host one leaf each and draw no switch. Tabs and leaves are keyed on their ids and neither list ever changes, so a body host is created ONCE and lives as long as the dock: the hidden leaves stay mounted, which is what keeps a half-typed value and the Assistant's transcript alive across a switch. `panels/right-panel.ts` keeps every decision — which leaf is selected, per document or detached; what the Page tab is called for this document; what the target's name is; and which seam a host is handed to.

style.$description: `styles/inspector.css`'s dock rules, carried in. Three of them were `#right-panel > .panel-*` — a direct-child selector that only held while this module rendered flat into the shell cell — and they are `[part]` rules on the document's own children now, which is the same statement without depending on how deep the dock is mounted. The header's typography is `panels.css`'s `.panel-header*`, at the same values: `--spectrum-font-size-50` resolved only inside `<sp-theme>` and a document mounts outside it, so it is `--jx-text-sm` (11px) here.

::before.$description: The separator between the tab's name and its target, drawn rather than written into the string — `panels/right-panel.ts` states what the dock is pointed at and nothing about punctuation.

& [part=\"tabs\"].$description: Three words in a 280px dock, allowed to compress rather than to become anonymous, which is why the tabs are not icons (§6). The kit tab's own 220px cap would let one tab push the last off the strip, so each takes an equal third.

& [part=\"panel\"].$description: `#right-panel > .panel-body { flex: 1; min-height: 0; overflow-y: auto }`, now a flex column: Element's sub-switch sits above its leaves and must not scroll away with them. The kit's tab panel pads itself for a dialog; a dock's tab is the whole column and each body pads its own content.

& [part=\"panel\"][hidden].$description: Out of sight, out of the layout and out of the accessibility tree, but not `display: none`: a panel that left the box tree is restyled whole when it comes back, and the Inspector shows its Page panel on every deselect and on every close of the Assistant (§6), which made each of those a 300-element style recalculation. `content-visibility: hidden` skips the subtree while keeping its computed style, so a return restyles only what changed while it was away; `visibility: hidden` keeps it unfocusable and unexposed, as `hidden` means.

& [part=\"subtabs\"].$description: Element's Content · Style · Logic switch. It is not a second tab strip: three views of the one selected node, so it is a single-select group inside the tab's body, and it does not count against the dock's four-tab cap (studio-ui-guidelines.md §12.2).

& [part=\"panel-body\"][data-tab=\"assis.$description: The chat owns its own scrolling, so its body is a flex column that does not scroll.

& [part=\"panel-body\"][data-active=\"fa.$description: A leaf that is not the one showing stays MOUNTED and is only taken out of the layout: it is a document with its own state, and rebuilding it on every switch would drop whatever it was holding. Hidden the way a hidden panel is (above), so switching back to it does not restyle it whole.

children.$description: The island. Every leaf is a mounted document of its own, so this stays EMPTY for the life of the dock — `panels/right-panel.ts` is handed it through `onNodeCreated` and passes it to that leaf's binder exactly once.
